topic: forging and tempering a mortise chisel: hearth heat, quench and an old worn anvil

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-1)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem

base: I have been forging a heavy mortise chisel from an old file and now I need to harden it properly.
There is also an older anvil in the shed, lighter and worn hollow, which my grandfather used daily.
I clamped a digital heat probe to the hearth wall, since it logs every reading for me.
The hearth runs hotter on one side, so the steel colours unevenly along the whole length.
Should I even out the fire first, or simply move the blade around while it heats?
Even out the fire first, because every judgement you make afterwards depends on seeing true colour.
A hot spot will bring one edge to cherry red while the rest is still dull.
Rake the coals into a deeper bed and let them settle for several minutes before working.
Only then does it make sense to judge the heat by eye rather than by time.
I banked the coals deeper and the whole blade now takes on the same even colour.
The quench left the edge hard, but the tang stayed soft and bends under hand pressure.
I worked on the older anvil that evening, and its hollow face may have absorbed my blows.
Does a soft tang matter, or is it actually useful for a tool struck with a mallet?
A soft tang is a virtue, since a fully hardened one would snap at the shoulder.
Quench only the working third and let the residual heat crawl back towards the edge slowly.
The hollow face of an old anvil returns less energy, so your blows feel dead and tiring.
For drawing out stock you want a face that rings, not one that swallows the hammer.
I quenched only the last third and the tang now flexes slightly without any sign of cracking.
The temper colours ran quickly, and I stopped them in water at a light straw shade.
The edge takes a keen bevel now, though it dulls faster than I honestly expected.
The heat probe logged a steady fire that evening, which makes the whole run easy to repeat.
Should I harden it again from scratch, or is a second tempering run enough to fix this?
Do not start again, because repeated cycles coarsen the grain and leave the steel more brittle.
A straw shade is on the hard side, so the edge should hold rather than crumble.
Rapid dulling usually means the bevel is too thin for the mortising work you are doing.
Try a slightly steeper grind first and give the same steel another week of honest use.
I reground the bevel steeper and the edge has survived a full week of chopping oak.
The older anvil still muffles every blow, so I have moved all my drawing work elsewhere.
Its face is dished by perhaps three millimetres in the middle, with the edges still sharp.
Is that worth grinding flat, or would I simply lose the hardened skin of the face?
You would lose the hardened skin, which on an old anvil is rarely thicker than a coin.
Three millimetres of dish is tolerable for most work, and many smiths never touch it.
Use the sharper edges for drawing out and keep the dished middle for gentler straightening.
If you must dress it, take off the least you can and stop at the first flat.
I will leave the face alone and use the sharper edge for drawing out from now on.
The chisel holds an edge through a whole afternoon of mortising, which is more than enough.
I would like to forge a matching narrower one before the winter draws in properly.
Should I use another old file, or start from a bar of plain tool steel?
Start from a known bar, because old files vary wildly and some are only case hardened.
A plain high carbon bar will behave the same way twice, which matters while you learn.
Forge the narrower blade slightly thicker and grind away the excess once it is tempered.
Keep a note of every heat and quench, so the next one is not guesswork again.
